content: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the anatomical structure that connects the lower jaw (mandible) to the skull, specifically the temporal bone. There are two TMJs, one on each side of the face, and they function in coordination to facilitate jaw movements. The joint derives its name from the two bones that form it: the temporal bone, which is part of the cranium, and the mandible. A unique feature of the TMJ is the presence of an articular disc, a fibrocartilaginous structure that acts as a cushion between the two bones. This disc divides the joint into two compartments: the lower compartment, which allows rotational movements (such as opening and closing the mouth), and the upper compartment, which permits translational movements (such as sliding the jaw forward or side to side). The mandibular condyle articulates with the articular disc, while the temporal bone's glenoid fossa interacts with the upper surface of the disc. The TMJ is classified as a ginglymoarthrodial joint, meaning it has both hinge-like (ginglymoid) and sliding (arthrodial) movements. During the initial phase of mouth opening, the condylar head rotates within the lower compartment of the joint. Once the mouth opens beyond approximately 20 millimeters, the upper compartment becomes active, and the condyle, along with the articular disc, translates forward and downward along the articular eminence of the temporal bone. This combined rotational and translational movement allows for a greater range of jaw opening. The TMJ consists of six primary components: the mandibular condyles, the articular surface of the temporal bone, the joint capsule, the articular disc, associated ligaments, and the lateral pterygoid muscle. The joint capsule is a fibrous membrane that encloses the joint and attaches to the articular eminence, the articular disc, and the neck of the mandibular condyle. The articular disc itself is a biconcave structure that divides the joint into two compartments and provides a smooth surface for articulation. The anterior portion of the disc is associated with the superior head of the lateral pterygoid muscle, while the posterior portion is connected to retrodiscal tissue, which is vascularized and innervated. Pain during jaw movement often arises when the condyle compresses this retrodiscal tissue, particularly in cases of anterior disc displacement. The TMJ is supported by three ligaments: the temporomandibular ligament, the stylomandibular ligament, and the sphenomandibular ligament. The temporomandibular ligament, the primary stabilizing structure, has two parts: an outer oblique portion and an inner horizontal portion. The stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments are accessory ligaments that help define the limits of mandibular movement. Excessive movement beyond these limits can result in pain due to overstretching of the associated tissues. The sensory innervation of the TMJ is provided by branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), specifically the auriculotemporal and masseteric nerves. The arterial blood supply to the joint primarily comes from the superficial temporal artery, a branch of the external carotid artery, with contributions from other branches such as the deep auricular, anterior tympanic, ascending pharyngeal, and maxillary arteries. Proprioception within the TMJ is mediated by specialized receptors, including Ruffini endings (static mechanoreceptors), Pacinian corpuscles (dynamic mechanoreceptors), Golgi tendon organs (protective static mechanoreceptors), and free nerve endings (pain receptors). Notably, the central portion of the articular disc lacks both innervation and vascularization, which prevents pain and bleeding during normal jaw movements. Jaw movements, collectively referred to as excursions, involve only the mandible. These movements include lateral excursions (to the left or right), protrusion (forward movement), and retrusion (backward movement). During protrusion, the mandibular incisors move edge-to-edge with the maxillary incisors and may even surpass them, creating a temporary underbite. This movement is achieved through translation of the condyle along the articular eminence. Chewing involves complex movements of the mandible, with the working side condyle performing rotation and the balancing side condyle undergoing translation. The four muscles of mastication—masseter, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid, and temporalis—coordinate these movements. The lateral pterygoid muscle is responsible for pulling the disc and condyle forward, facilitating mouth opening, while the other three muscles close the mouth. The most common disorder affecting the TMJ is disc displacement, where the articular disc moves out of its normal position between the condyle and the temporal bone. This displacement is often anterior and can result in pain due to compression of the retrodiscal tissue. In cases of disc displacement with reduction, a click or pop sound is heard as the condyle moves back onto the disc during jaw opening. In contrast, disc displacement without reduction is characterized by limited mouth opening and the absence of clicking sounds. TMJ pain can arise from several causes, including myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome (involving the muscles of mastication), internal derangements (such as disc displacement), and degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis). Additionally, TMJ pain is a recognized diagnostic criterion for temporal arteritis.
